introduction.text: **Before you start.** Until now the program asked for food that is cooked well and served hot. This course adds intent to how it looks:

items.text: **composition:** colour, height, negative space, a focal point, odd numbers; the plate's size, shape and colour; portions that fit the course;
**saucing and garnish:** pools, lines and dots, sauce at the table, and garnish that is edible and adds flavour;
**styles:** classical, family-style and modern, and which suits which occasion;
**photography for evidence:** a photo corner that makes every later photo reliable for AI review and for your own record.

introduction.text: Plating serves the food: a plate is judged hot and good to eat first, then composed. The dishes are your own repertoire, cooked with Dutch seasonal produce, so the course costs little beyond household meals.
Plan about two weeks at 6.5 hours a week, or run it alongside another S4 course: each lesson is plated on household meals, with two guest dinners.

**Have ready:** plain white plates in three sizes, and a bowl; one dark plate if you have one; a platter and serving bowls with a spoon for each; two spoons, a small offset spatula and a squeeze bottle; a damp cloth for rims; the instant-read probe; paper and a pencil for sketches; for the photo corner, a window, a plain matt grey or white board, a white card, a phone stand, a ruler or the grid board.

note.text: **Knowledge check:** the 8 items of `PLT-4.M1` in the course file. Pass mark 80 %.

blocks.text: **Why it matters:** a few principles decide whether a plate reads clearly or looks crowded. Sketching the plate first, and plating it hot and fast, lets you choose the look instead of finding it by accident.

**You need:** a household main course with at least three components (for example a fish, a seasonal vegetable purée and glazed vegetables); three warm plates of the same kind; the probe; two spoons and an offset spatula; paper for three sketches; a phone for photos.
**Explanation:**
*The principles:*

items.text: **colour:** contrast between the components (green against brown, white against dark). The colour comes from the food, not from decoration.
**height:** a little height draws the eye and shows care. Lean the components against each other; don't build towers that fall.
**negative space:** empty plate around the food, so it reads clearly; on a composed plate, leave about a third of the plate free.
**focal point:** one place the eye goes first, usually the main item, often slightly off-centre.
**odd numbers:** three or five pieces look natural; even numbers look arranged.
**flow:** place the components so the guest can eat them together, in the order you intend.

blocks.text: *The sketch.* Draw the plate from above before you plate: where each item goes, how large, and the empty space.
*Hot food first.* Warm the plates to about 60 °C, in a low oven, or with hot water and then dried. Plate fast; the plate leaves within a minute. A beautiful cold plate of hot food is a failure.
Three layouts to sketch:

rows: The main item in the middle, the rest around it
The main item a third of the way across, sauce and garnish leading to it
The components in a line or a gentle curve

blocks.text: **Practice:**

items.text: **One dish three ways (60 min).** Plate a household main course three ways from three sketches: centred, off-centre and linear. Photograph each from above and at 45°, and compare.

blocks.text: **Look for:**

items.text: a clear focal point in each version;
the food hot when the photo is taken.

blocks.text: **If it goes wrong:**

rows: Leave about a third free; use a larger plate
A stack that topples on the way
Lean components; keep height low and stable

blocks.text: **Safety:** plates warmed in a low oven handled with dry cloths; hot food kept hot until plated, at 57 °C or above if it waits (assessment §9).
**Record:** the three sketches next to the three photos; which you prefer and why.

**Why it matters:** the same food looks lost on one plate and crowded on another, and a menu of large portions tires a guest before dessert. The plate and the portion are choices you make for the whole menu.
**You need:** a starter of your repertoire; three plates of different size and colour (a large white, a small white, a dark or coloured one); the scale; a phone for photos.
**Explanation:**
*The plate.*

items.text: White and plain shows food best; dark plates suit pale food.
A wide rim frames a small portion.
A bowl holds sauce and keeps food warm.
Match the size to the portion: a starter on a large plate looks lost; a main course on a small plate looks crowded.

blocks.text: *Shape.* Round plates for most food; rectangular or oval for long items (a whole fish, a slice of terrine).
*Portion size for the course.* Judge the portion against the whole menu, not only the dish:

rows: 150–200 g of protein, with vegetables and starch

blocks.text: Weigh the main item the first time, so your eye learns what 100 g looks like on a plate.

*Judging the menu.* Write the portions of every course in a column and read them together. If the starter is rich, make the main course lighter or smaller; if the main course is large, keep the dessert small. A guest should finish every course and still want the next.
**Practice:**

items.text: **Plate choices (60 min).** Put the same starter on three plates of different size and colour. Photograph each, and write which you would choose and why.

blocks.text: **Look for:** your choice of plate and portion has a reason a guest would see.
**If it goes wrong:**

rows: A large portion on every course
Plan the portions across the menu
Plain plates; dark only for pale food

blocks.text: **Safety:** none beyond the kitchen routine: hot food kept hot, cold food cold (assessment §9).
**Record:** the three photos; the plate you chose and the portion weight.

exercises.title: One dish plated three ways
exercises.description: One dish plated three ways; photos compared.

blocks.text: **Task:** plate a composed dish deliberately from a sketch, and learn from comparing versions. Plate one composed dish three ways from three sketches, served hot, and compare the photos against the composition checklist.
**You need:** a household main course with at least three components (for example a fish, a seasonal vegetable purée and glazed vegetables); warm plates; the probe; a phone.
**Framework:** the composition checklist.

rows: One place the eye goes first, as sketched
The main item probed on the plate

blocks.text: *Procedure:*

items.text: Draw three sketches: focal point, colour contrast, height.
Plate each version; probe the main item on the plate; photograph each from above and at 45°.
Compare the photos with the sketches; choose the best and write why.

blocks.text: **Show:** a plate designed from a sketch for a composed dish, with focal point, colour contrast and height as sketched, served hot (the probe reading on the plate), as the `TS-PLT` level 3 row asks.

AI review reads the sketches, the photos and the probe readings: *competent* is plates that match their sketches on every point of the checklist, served hot; *not yet* is a plate without a clear focal point, food to the rim, or no probe reading.

items.question: What is negative space on a plate?

options.text: the dark part of the food
the empty plate around the food, which lets it read clearly

items.question: Why are three scallops placed rather than four?
Where is the focal point usually placed?

options.text: the main item, often slightly off-centre

items.why: One place the eye goes first.

items.question: Your plate looks beautiful in the photo, but the guest found the food lukewarm. What went wrong, and what changes?
items.answer: Plating took too long on a cold plate. Warm the plates, prepare the sketch and tools first, and plate within a minute.

items.question: Which is a good use of height?

options.text: components leaning against each other, a little height

items.question: A small starter on a large white plate with a wide rim: what does the rim do?
A four-course menu: everyone was full after the main. What do you change in the portions?
items.answer: Smaller starter and main (for example 80–120 g for the starter and 150 g of protein in the main), a small intense dessert, judged against the whole menu.

items.question: Which plate suits a pale white fish with a cream sauce?

note.text: **Knowledge check:** none for this module. Its one judgment objective (garnish with purpose) is shown on the guests' cards and plates of `PLT-4.M2.X1`.

blocks.text: **Why it matters:** where the sauce goes changes how a dish eats as much as how it looks. A garnish that adds flavour earns its place; one that only adds colour is left on the plate.

**You need:** about 300 ml of one sauce (a vegetable purée, a reduction or a fluid gel from `MOD-4.M3.L2`); ten white plates; spoons of two sizes; a squeeze bottle; a small jug; a damp cloth; for the guest course, a course of your repertoire for four.
**Explanation:**
*Sauce placement:*

items.text: **pool:** under or beside the main item, spooned and tilted to spread; for sauces the item sits in;
**line or swoosh:** a spoonful dragged with the back of the spoon; for thick sauces and purées;
**dots:** from a squeeze bottle, for intense sauces in small amounts (a reduction, a fluid gel);
**at the table:** poured from a jug in front of the guest, for sauces that would spoil a crisp skin or set (*beurre blanc*, a consommé over a garnish).

blocks.text: *Clean edges.* Wipe the rim with a damp cloth or paper. Never put sauce under a crisp skin.
*The amount.* Enough sauce to go with every bite, no more: about 40–60 ml for a main course.
*Every garnish is edible and adds flavour.*

items.text: A herb leaf that belongs to the dish.
A crisp that adds texture (`MOD-4.M5`).
A pickle that adds acid (`PRS-3`).

blocks.text: No inedible decoration, and no garnish that only adds colour.
**Practice:**

items.text: **Saucing drill (60 min).** Place one sauce ten ways on ten plates: pools, lines, swooshes, dots, and one poured at the table. Photograph them together.
**A course for guests (60 min).** Use the best saucing and a purposeful garnish on a course for four.

blocks.text: **Look for:**

items.text: clean, deliberate lines and pools;
every garnish eaten, and mentioned on the cards.

blocks.text: **If it goes wrong:**

rows: Sauce under or over the crisp skin
Sauce beside it, or at the table
Same bottle, same pressure, same height
Wipe with a damp cloth before it leaves

blocks.text: **Safety:** sauces kept hot at 57 °C or above until plated, or cold at 5 °C or below (assessment §9); a herb garnish washed and dried.
**Record:** the drill photo with the best three marked; the course photo; what the guests said about the garnish.

exercises.title: Saucing practice: one sauce, ten ways
exercises.description: Saucing practice on plates with one sauce, ten ways.

blocks.text: **Task:** control sauce placement, and use it on a course for guests. Place one sauce ten ways (pools, lines, dots, sauce at the table). Then use the best placement on a course designed with a sketch and plated for at least four guests, the plates matching and hot.
**You need:** one sauce (a purée, a reduction or a fluid gel) for the drill; a course of your repertoire for the guests; the plates and tools; the probe; guest cards.
**Recipe:** the saucing reference sheet.

rows: Poured in front of the guest
Sauces that spoil a crisp skin or set

blocks.text: *Procedure:*

items.text: Plate the ten versions; photograph them together; mark the best three.
Sketch the guest course with the chosen saucing.
Plate it for four or more guests; probe one plate; photograph the plates together.
Collect guest cards.

blocks.text: **Show:** the drill photos, and course two of three of the `TS-PLT` level 4 row: sketched, plated for at least four guests, the plates matching, hot, and judged by the AI review and the guests as composed with intent. The first course is in `PST-4.M5.X1`, the third in `PLT-4.M3.X1`.

AI review reads the drill photo, the sketch, the plate photos, the probe reading and the cards: *competent* is clean placements, four matching plates that follow the sketch, served hot; *not yet* is smears or uneven dots, plates that differ, or no probe reading.
**Time:** 2 h.

note.text: **Knowledge check:** the 8 items of `PLT-4.M3` in the course file, 1 of them a safety item. Pass mark 80 %, with every safety item correct.

blocks.text: **Why it matters:** the same food can be served in three styles, and each suits a different table. Knowing them, and how to send out a platter that guests can serve from safely, lets you choose the style for the occasion.

**You need:** a household main course (a roast or a braise with seasonal vegetables); a platter and serving bowls, warmed; a carving knife and board; a serving spoon for every dish; a small jug for the sauce.
**Explanation:**
*The three styles:*

items.text: **classical:** the main item at the front, the garnish arranged around it, the sauce beside or under; the plate ordered and symmetrical (`CLS-4.M5`);
**family-style:** platters and bowls on the table, guests serving themselves; generous, warm and relaxed, the food arranged to look abundant and easy to serve;
**modern:** a composed plate built in the kitchen, often asymmetric, with height, negative space and several textures; one idea per plate (`PST-4.M5`, `MOD-4`).

blocks.text: *Platters and shared dishes:*

items.text: warm the platter;
carve or portion the main item before it goes out, so guests can serve themselves easily;
put the sauce in a jug and the garnish in its own bowl, or scatter it over;
give every dish its own serving spoon;
keep allergen-free dishes apart, each with its own spoon, and tell the guest which they are (`NUT-3`).

blocks.text: *The idea behind the plate* (`CR-COMP`). One sentence says what the dish is about, and every style keeps it.
**Practice:**

items.text: **A family-style platter (60 min).** Serve a main course for the household on a platter with shared bowls, and photograph the table.

blocks.text: **Look for:**

items.text: a platter that looks generous and is easy to serve from;
each style recognisable in the photos.

blocks.text: **If it goes wrong:**

rows: A whole joint sent out uncut
Carve it in the kitchen; arrange the slices
An allergen reaches the wrong plate
A spoon per dish; allergen-free dishes apart

blocks.text: **Safety:** a spoon per dish, allergen-free dishes kept apart with their own spoons and named to the guest (`NUT-3`); food on the table eaten within the meal, and leftovers cooled and kept by the leftover rows (assessment §9).
**Record:** the table photo; the idea of the dish in one sentence.
**Why it matters:** choosing the style is a judgment about the guests, the occasion and the cook's time. Plating one dish three ways shows that the idea stays while the presentation changes.
**You need:** a main course of your repertoire with three or more components; a platter and bowls; two plates; the plating tools; a sketch for the modern plate; a phone.
**Explanation:**
*One dish in each style.* Plate the same components classically, family-style and modern. For example, a braised beef with root vegetables and a sauce:

rows: Slices at the front, vegetables turned and arranged behind, sauce under the meat
Sliced on a platter in its sauce, vegetables in a bowl, sauce in a jug
One piece off-centre, a root vegetable purée swooshed, crisp vegetable shards for height

blocks.text: *Which suits which occasion:*

items.text: a family dinner or a crowd: family-style (warmer, quicker, less washing-up, guests choose their portions);
a formal dinner or a celebration: plated (classical or modern), each guest served the same;
a dish whose texture or temperature must be exact (a soufflé, a seared scallop): plated in the kitchen;
the cook's time: plating for eight takes help or practice (`MNU-4.M3`).

blocks.text: *The idea stays the same.* Whatever the style, the dish's idea and flavours are the same; only the presentation changes. Write the idea first, then check each version against it in the photos.
**Practice:**

items.text: **One dish, three styles (60 min).** Plate a dish in each style, photograph each, and write the occasion it suits.

blocks.text: **Look for:** each version suits a named occasion, and the same idea is clear in all three.
**If it goes wrong:**

rows: Every course plated for a casual meal
Served from pans on the table
Plate it, or use proper platters

blocks.text: **Safety:** plating three versions takes time: keep the food hot at 57 °C or above while you work (assessment §9), and serve the household the version plated last.
**Record:** the three photos with their occasions; the dish's idea in one sentence.

exercises.title: A family dinner and a formal dinner
exercises.description: The same main course for a family dinner and for a formal dinner.

blocks.text: **Task:** present the same main course for two occasions, keeping its idea: a family dinner (family-style) and a formal dinner (plated). Design the formal version with a sketch and plate it for at least four guests, the plates matching and hot. Compose both versions with a written idea for their menu.
**You need:** a main course of your repertoire with seasonal Dutch vegetables; platters and plates; the probe; household and guest cards.
*Procedure:*

items.text: Write the idea of the dish and of each version; sketch the formal plate.
Serve the family dinner; photograph the table; collect household cards.
Serve the formal dinner for at least four; probe one plate; photograph the plates together; collect guest cards.
Write what each version kept and changed.

blocks.text: **Show:**

items.text: **`TS-PLT` level 4, course three of three:** the formal plate sketched and plated for at least four guests, matching and hot. With `PST-4.M5.X1` and `PLT-4.M2.X1`, the three courses are complete; the photos are re-taken for AI review in `PLT-4.M4.X1`.
**`CR-COMP` level 4, dishes two and three:** two compositions with a written idea, each element serving it in the photos and cards. With `PST-4.M5.X1`, the row is complete.

blocks.text: AI review reads the ideas, the sketch, the photos, the probe reading and the cards: *competent* is two versions that keep one idea, a formal plate that follows the sketch on four matching hot plates, and a platter that is easy to serve from; *not yet* is an idea lost in one version, plates that differ, or no probe reading.
**Time:** 2 dinners of about 2.5 h.

options.text: platters and bowls on the table, guests serving themselves

items.question: Which is typical of the modern style?

options.text: the garnish around the main item in order
an asymmetric composed plate with height and space

items.question: A roast goes out family-style. How?

options.text: carved before it goes out, with the sauce in a jug

items.question: A guest has a sesame allergy and dinner is family-style. What do you do?

options.text: keep the sesame-free dishes apart, each with its own spoon, and tell the guest which they are
skip sesame in one dish only

items.question: You cook for twelve relatives on a Sunday, alone. Which style, and why?
items.answer: Family-style: quicker for one cook, keeps the food hot, guests choose their portions.
items.why: [J] the occasion and the cook's time.

items.question: For a celebration dinner for six you serve seared scallops as a starter. Plated or shared? Why?
items.answer: Plated in the kitchen: the sear and the temperature must be exact and every guest served the same.

items.question: What stays the same when a dish changes style?
What is the risk of plating every course at a casual meal for many?

options.text: the food waits and cools while one cook plates

items.why: Plating for many takes time or help.

note.text: **Knowledge check:** none for this module. It has no knowledge or judgment objective; the photos are checked against the evidence checklist.

blocks.text: **Why it matters:** AI review and your own record compare photos over months. A change of light, angle or background can look like a change in the food, so a consistent set-up makes the evidence reliable (assessment §6).

**You need:** a window with daylight and no direct sun; a plain, matt grey or white board; a white card (A4 or larger); a phone stand; a ruler or the grid board; a sharp knife and a damp cloth; three dishes to photograph.
**Explanation:**
*The photo corner:*

items.text: **daylight** from one side (a window), no direct sun and no kitchen lamps mixed in; a white card opposite softens the shadows;
**background:** a plain, matt surface, such as a grey or white board;
**angles:** from above (90°) for composition, at 45° for height, level for layers and cross-sections;
**scale:** a ruler or the grid board in the frame for cuts, crumbs and portions;
**the camera:** a phone on a stand at a fixed distance, the lens wiped, no zoom, no filters.

blocks.text: Photograph the set-up itself once it works, with the stand's position marked, so you can rebuild it the same way.
*Cross-sections.* Cut with a sharp, clean knife, wiped between cuts, and photograph level and at once.
*The evidence checklist.*

items.text: Light: daylight from one side, nothing mixed in.
Angle: the one the evidence asks for.
Background: plain and matt.
Scale: in the frame where size matters.
Focus: sharp on the food.
File name: the date and the exercise ID, for example `2026-11-20_PLT-4.M4.X1_1.jpg`.

blocks.text: *Reviewing the record.* Look through your photos since S1 for a pattern: what makes some hard to judge? Then write a plan to fix it.
**Practice:**

items.text: **Setting up the corner (60 min).** Build the corner. Take three test shots and check them against the checklist. Photograph the set-up so you can repeat it.
**Re-shoots (60 min).** Re-shoot three dishes in the corner, including a cross-section.

blocks.text: **Look for:**

items.text: photos that pass every point of the checklist;
the same light and angle on different days.

blocks.text: **If it goes wrong:**

rows: A sharp knife, wiped between cuts

blocks.text: **Safety:** hot food photographed quickly and then served or cooled by the cooling rule (assessment §9); the knife wiped and laid flat.
**Record:** the set-up photo; the test shots with their checklist; the three re-shoots.

exercises.title: A photo corner and three dishes re-shot
exercises.description: Set up a photo corner and re-shoot three dishes.

blocks.text: **Task:** make every later photo reliable as evidence, and check two practice plans against your record. Set up a photo corner and re-shoot three dishes in it. The three dishes are the three courses of the `TS-PLT` level 4 row (from `PST-4.M5.X1`, `PLT-4.M2.X1` and `PLT-4.M3.X1`), cooked again and photographed for the AI review. Review your photo record since S1 for a pattern across at least ten entries (what made photos hard to judge), with a practice plan that the re-shoots show worked. Check the doneness plan of `PRO-4.M6.X1` against the cross-sections taken since.
**You need:** a window, a plain board, a white card, the phone stand, the grid; the three courses.
**Recipe:** the evidence checklist of `PLT-4.M4.L1` (light, angle, background, scale, focus, file name).
*Procedure:*

items.text: Review at least ten earlier evidence photos against the checklist; write the pattern and the plan.
Set up the corner; take the test shots; record the set-up.
Cook and re-shoot the three courses, with a cross-section where it applies.
Check the doneness plan of `PRO-4.M6.X1` against the cross-sections since; write whether it worked.

blocks.text: **Show:**

items.text: **`TS-PLT` level 4, the AI-review photos:** the three courses in consistent evidence photos, judged by the AI review as composed with intent; the guests' judgment was given at the dinners.

**`JD-REFL` level 4, the plans checked:** a pattern across ten photo entries and a plan that the re-shoots show worked; the doneness plan of `PRO-4.M6.X1` checked against the later entries. `MNU-4.M5.X1` and `MS-S4.M1.L6` complete the row.

blocks.text: AI review reads the review notes, the set-up photo and the re-shoots: *competent* is a pattern named from ten entries, re-shoots that pass every point of the checklist with matching light and angle, and a written check of the doneness plan; *not yet* is fewer than ten entries, mixed light or a busy background, or no check of the plan.
**Time:** 3 h.
